title: Cerebral's CMD-1 crisis-message detector cuts median time to crisis-specialist triage from about 9 hours to 8–13 minutes in a prospective October 2022 deployment
summary: Cerebral's CMD-1 crisis-message detector screened 102,471 patient chat messages in October 2022 and cut the daily median time to crisis-specialist triage to 8 to 13 minutes from over 9 hours.
account: Cerebral Inc., a national tele-mental-health provider, worked with Stanford University School of Medicine on Crisis Message Detector 1 (CMD-1). CMD-1 is a two-stage natural-language-processing system: key-word filtering, then logistic regression. It flags patient chat messages indicating possible suicidal or homicidal ideation, domestic violence or non-suicidal self-injury. It surfaces them to Cerebral's crisis specialists via a Slack interface. The model was trained on 721 messages (32% potential crises) sent between 1 April 2021 and 1 April 2022. On a retrospective test set of 481 messages, it reached an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.82, a sensitivity of 0.99 and a positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.35. CMD-1 then ran in Cerebral's production systems from 1 October to 31 October 2022 as a prospective validation. The prospective test set had 102,471 messages from that month, and 9,795 of these passed the key-word filter. On that set, CMD-1 reached an AUC of 0.98, a sensitivity of 0.98 and a PPV of 0.66. In the prospective period the daily median time from message receipt to crisis-specialist triage was 8 to 13 minutes. Before deployment it averaged more than 9 hours, per Cerebral's internal analysis. False negatives reached specialists through usual channels. Swaminathan, López and colleagues, of Cerebral and Stanford, published these results in npj Digital Medicine on 21 November 2023. Seven authors report salary and equity in Cerebral and three part-time employment there. Stanford HAI's account of 8 January 2024 gives the reduction as “from 10 hours to under 10 minutes” with 97% sensitivity and specificity. Those figures differ slightly from the paper's. The authors report no downstream patient outcome, such as hospitalization, emergency department use or suicide attempts. As of 29 October 2026, no independent study has measured the system, and no source reports whether Cerebral kept using it after that month.

ai_role.statement: The classifier decides which messages are surfaced to crisis specialists, who then triage them. Humans labeled the outcomes. fields.summary: Cerebral's CMD-1 crisis-message detector screened 102,471 patient chat messages in October 2022 and cut the daily median time to crisis-specialist triage to 8 to 13 minutes from over 9 hours.
fields.account: Cerebral Inc., a national tele-mental-health provider, worked with Stanford University School of Medicine on Crisis Message Detector 1 (CMD-1). CMD-1 is a two-stage natural-language-processing system: key-word filtering, then logistic regression. It flags patient chat messages indicating possible suicidal or homicidal ideation, domestic violence or non-suicidal self-injury. It surfaces them to Cerebral's crisis specialists via a Slack interface. The model was trained on 721 messages (32% potential crises) sent between 1 April 2021 and 1 April 2022. On a retrospective test set of 481 messages, it reached an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.82, a sensitivity of 0.99 and a positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.35. CMD-1 then ran in Cerebral's production systems from 1 October to 31 October 2022 as a prospective validation. The prospective test set had 102,471 messages from that month, and 9,795 of these passed the key-word filter. On that set, CMD-1 reached an AUC of 0.98, a sensitivity of 0.98 and a PPV of 0.66. In the prospective period the daily median time from message receipt to crisis-specialist triage was 8 to 13 minutes. Before deployment it averaged more than 9 hours, per Cerebral's internal analysis. False negatives reached specialists through usual channels. Swaminathan, López and colleagues, of Cerebral and Stanford, published these results in npj Digital Medicine on 21 November 2023. Seven authors report salary and equity in Cerebral and three part-time employment there. Stanford HAI's account of 8 January 2024 gives the reduction as “from 10 hours to under 10 minutes” with 97% sensitivity and specificity. Those figures differ slightly from the paper's. The authors report no downstream patient outcome, such as hospitalization, emergency department use or suicide attempts. As of 29 October 2026, no independent study has measured the system, and no source reports whether Cerebral kept using it after that month.
